Photograph: NPS/Alamy Arizona Remote Grand Canyon lodge hit by deadly flash flood boasts fabled history Phantom Ranch, set up by Teddy Roosevelt, has welcomed exhausted hikers to its famed cabins for over a century Two dead and nearly 80 rescued after Grand Canyon flash flood Joanna Walters Mon 31 Aug 2026 21.54 EDT First published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 17.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Phantom Ranch has been a solitary refuge visited by some of the most famous names of history. More typically, it’s been a beacon for the half-collapsed, exhausted and overheated hikers trudging down the Grand Canyon for more than a century. Two dead and at least 15 missing after flash flood in Arizona’s Grand Canyon Read more The sole lodge at the very bottom of the Grand Canyon, the cabins long had a near mythical reputation. Located along the Bright Angel Creek, which tumbles into the mighty Colorado River at the base of the canyon, they served as a reminder of the long history of one of America’s most spectacular but savage environments. It’s unclear yet how much damage the lodge has sustained after Saturday’s lethal flash flood . On Saturday afternoon, more than 60 people had to be evacuated by air from the ranch and the bottom of the adjacent North Kaibab Trail, which winds 14 miles down from the lesser-trodden North Rim of the canyon. Two people were confirmed dead, nearly 80 people were rescued and one person remained unaccounted for. Native Americans have made their home in various parts of the canyon for thousands of years and were driven out of much – though not all – of it before US president Theodore Roosevelt declared the canyon a national monument in 1908. It was Roosevelt who set up a camp on the site where the little visitor lodge now stands, while he was on a hunting trip in 1913. The area became a national park in 1919 and the ranch, named after one of the many side canyons within the Grand Canyon, opened in 1922. Boaters floating and paddling down the Colorado River stay there, as do people riding mules. The future King Gustaf VI Adolf of Sweden was a prominent early guest, arriving via mule, in 1926. In 1967, then senator Robert F Kennedy stayed at Phantom Ranch beneath the towering canyon walls after rafting down the Colorado with family and friends, bouncing and gliding 90 miles on the east-west flow of the river from Lake Powell. Today, more than a vertical mile above, the hundreds of thousands of visitors who just peep over the South Rim, where lodges, tourist information spots, shops and restaurants buzz, cannot see the river, let alone the tiny ranch so far below. But hikers who trek down the seven or eight zig-zag miles of the nearby dusty South Kaibab or Bright Angel trails to the bottom and cross footbridges over the Colorado to reach the ranch descend steadily from tourist hullabaloo into an ever more rugged and tranquil wilderness. Here, heat, thirst or flood are the biggest dangers, not the resident mountain lions, rattlesnakes or scorpions. Having pounded the hard rock paths and rough steps all the way down, the few who get to stay at the ranch or snag a campsite along the creek are mostly thinking of the relief of not having to climb back up to the rim yet and the magic of cooling their throbbing feet in a stream before a simple canteen meal at communal tables and a rudimentary bed for a night or two. But that sense of safety can be as elusively spectral as the name of the refuge. A fast and fierce deluge, such as occurred at the weekend, can quickly form a roaring flash flood when the rain swells creeks that drop steeply into the canyon as tributaries to the Colorado, which is what just happened in the Bright Angel Creek. The National Park Service describes flash flooding as an inherent risk in the canyon but had additionally warned in February of “the elevated potential for flash flooding and debris flows in the Bright Angel Creek watershed” following the Dragon Bravo wildfire that decimated parts of the North Rim last year and forced the closure of the North Kaibab trail from July to March of this year. https://www.politico.eu/article/seven-mi.text: Seven crew members are missing after a tanker caught fire close to Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea Thursday morning, Romanian authorities said. The San Marino-flagged chemical tanker sent a distress call at 7 a.m. local time about 13 nautical miles from Sulina, a port on Romania’s eastern coast, close to the Ukrainian border. Romanian border police, along with aviation units, arrived to assist the crew, the Romanian Naval Authority said . Five people have been rescued so far, the naval authority told local media . Another tanker was affected by a fire late on Wednesday close to Sulina, with authorities confirming the crew were safe. Advertisement Advertisement Romanian authorities have not given a reason for either incident. The fires broke out hours after the country’s defense ministry announced an air alert around Snake Island — a Ukrainian territory located about 40 kilometers from the spot where the San Marino tanker sent its distress signal. A drone was also spotted near Sulina overnight `”after which it disappeared from the radar,” the ministry wrote. At least five commercial vessels have been hit by suspected drone strikes in the Black Sea over the past two weeks. The deadly attacks are affecting a key route that carries 95% of Ukraine’s grain exports . On Oct. 6, drones struck two ships in Bulgaria’s Black Sea economic zone. One sank, and its 10 crew members went missing. On Tuesday two more ships were struck near Bulgaria , leaving 11 crew members missing. Romanian President Nicusor Dan will meet Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte for talks on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels at 1:30 p.m. today.

Photograph: 34th Separate Marine Brigade 'Borysfen'/Reuters Ukraine Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds Pjotr Sauer and Peter Beaumont Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.10 EDT First published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 29 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations. Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire. The White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump , and her representative worked directly with ​Russian and Ukrainian ‌leadership to define the ​terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said. Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls. Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe . As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement. Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town. Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network , despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service. The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries. The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place. “I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters. Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted. “At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy. “There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added. The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days. Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel , as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday. Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month. The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement. Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row? Read more Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership. Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said. The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion. https://cphpost.dk/2026-10-15/global/nor.text: A 50-year-old Ukrainian man accused of leading the 2022 attacks on gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea appeared in a Hamburg courtroom as his lawyer called for the charges to be dismissed. The defendant, identified by German media as Serhii K., will not testify because of confidentiality obligations linked to his former service in Ukraine’s special forces, his lawyer said. Defense attorney Nicola Canestrini argued that prosecutors lacked clear evidence connecting his client to the explosions. He also accused Russia of using the pipelines to exert political and economic pressure. “They were a means of exerting pressure in a war,” Canestrini said, according to Reuters. Serhii K. faces charges including complicity in war crimes, disrupting public utilities, causing explosions and destroying structures. German prosecutors allege that he led a group responsible for sabotaging the Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022. According to the indictment, the group traveled aboard a yacht rented in Rostock, Germany, before reaching waters near the Danish island of Bornholm and planting explosives. Prosecutors also allege that Serhii K. traveled through Poland to Germany using a false passport months before the attacks. He was arrested in Italy last year. Supporters gathered outside the courthouse, questioning the war crimes allegations against him. “Russia is the only war criminal that belongs in the dock,” one protester told Reuters. Russia has denied involvement in the explosions, although several Western countries initially suspected Moscow. The pipelines, built by Russian energy company Gazprom, lie 80 to 110 meters beneath the Baltic Sea. The trial is expected to continue until February.
